title: The pump that won't run
oneLine: On a DOL starter's control circuit, start with what changed, make it dead and prove it, choose tests that each clear about half of what is left, test a contact the way it is used, and prove start, hold and every Stop before the job is done.
skill: Find a fault on a DOL control circuit from a report: choose the first move and say how sure you are; put isolation and proving dead in order; judge live against dead testing; predict, then read, dead continuity tests; split the coil's path in half; test Start held in and Stop held pressed; read a coil's rating against how it is fed; name the fault and its kind; prove the fix; explain it to a new hand in plain words.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 9)
materialRefs: nvq-fault-finding p.2 (an approach to fault finding; questions to ask, including the events which led to the fault; visual inspection first)
nvq-fault-finding p.4 (fault kinds: open circuit, short circuit, high resistance; tests to detect them: an approved voltage indicator for voltage, a low resistance ohmmeter for open circuits)
nvq-fault-finding p.6 (leaving safe: isolate what cannot be repaired, tell the person who ordered the work in writing)
nvq-health-safety p.2 (safe re-energisation: loads disconnected so nothing starts unexpectedly)
hsg85 p.7-8 (paras 23-24: the three conditions for live work; fault-finding named as a case where dead may be unreasonable: taught as a judgement)
hsg85 p.12 (para 38: accidents during fault-finding under pressure to repair)
hsg85 p.14-16 (paras 46-55: identify, disconnect, secure isolation, notices, prove dead, test the instrument before and after use)
s-plan-fault-finding, y-plan-fault-finding (his own step-by-step voltage tracing charts: a piece-by-piece route to contrast with halving; not shown)

to research: half-splitting as a fault-finding method; proving the fix by a functional test of start, hold and every Stop; a joint that bridges a remote Stop after a cable repair; a Stop that does not work keeps the equipment out of use until it is found; a general source for a contactor coil's operating band (85% to 110% of rated coil voltage); whether a wrongly rated coil buzzes or stays silent
picture: The bench: the control circuit as a vertical ladder from supply to neutral: P0, control fuse, P1, panel Stop, P2, a two-core cable with its repair joint out to the pump's Stop between R1 and R2 and back, P3, Start with the hold-in contact 13-14 across it, P4, overload contact 95-96, P5, coil A1-A2, N; the motor drawn faint beside it. Put the leads on any two points and the meter shows near zero, a coil's reading or over range, computed from the circuit and the hidden fault; toggles hold Start in and hold the pump's Stop pressed. A warm-up and three jobs: no click; a Stop that won't stop; after a contactor change.
builds_on: Motors lesson 2 (the DOL starter: Stops in series, the hold-in contact across Start, no-volt protection, coil voltage)
Your trade: safe isolation, continuity and voltage testing, contactors and overloads

title: The motor that hums, trips or runs hot
oneLine: On a motor's power circuit, the three line currents, the line voltages and an insulation reading together tell a burnt contact pole from a binding load, an overload set wrong or wet windings; the insulation minimums in use disagree, and both are shown as a disagreement.
skill: Use a clamp meter on each line, line-to-line voltage and an insulation tester to separate single-phasing from a burnt main contact, a binding load from an overload set wrong, and low insulation after standing wet; know which tests need the motor running and which need it dead; know why the minimum insulation figures differ.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 9)
materialRefs: nvq-fault-finding p.3-4 (common faults: component failure such as contactors, insulation failure, excess current; tests: insulation resistance with 1 to 2 megohms as a possible latent fault and below 1 megohm as a likely fault, a clamp meter on an energised working circuit)

Motors research, checked quotes reused by number: [32], [34] (worn contacts the commonest cause of single-phasing), [106] (moisture after standing idle), [227] (173% in the remaining two lines), [228], [229], [230] (IEEE 43 minimum of 1 megohm plus 1 per kV), [232] (5 megohms up to 1,000 V, as one maker cites it)
Subsea research (insulation resistance over time, polarisation index) where it carries over
to research: setting an overload to the motor's full-load current; what a binding load does to the current over time; the live tests a clamp needs, judged as in lesson 1
picture: The power circuit: supply, main contacts, overload, motor terminals, with a clamp on each line, line-to-line voltage and an insulation tester. Jobs: hums, won't turn, then trips (a burnt main contact pole); trips after running a while (a binding pump, against an overload set wrong); trips at once after standing wet (low insulation resistance on the windings). Every reading computed from a shown rule or shown as a class; the two insulation minimums side by side.
builds_on: Design and verification lesson 3 (overload setting against design current)

title: The earth fault that doesn't trip
oneLine: On an insulated ship's supply, a first earth fault raises an alarm but trips nothing, so it is found by switching sections off one at a time while essential services keep running, and a second earth on another line is the dangerous one, because it makes a short circuit through the hull.
skill: Read earth lamps or an insulation monitor to tell which line has gone to earth; plan sectionalising so essential services stay on; explain why a second earth on another line is dangerous and why the first must be found; say how this differs from automatic disconnection on a shore supply.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 9)
materialRefs: None of his materials cover insulated ship's systems: public sources only, never how the Royal Navy does it
AC circuits research [43] (most ships use a three-phase, three-wire, 440 V insulated neutral system)

to research: earth lamps and insulation monitors on an insulated system; what a first and a second earth fault do; sectionalising a board to find an earth while keeping essential services; the classification society or IEC rules on earth fault indication; the MCA electro-technical officer syllabus lines on earth faults
picture: An insulated 440 V three-wire board with earth lamps or an insulation monitor and six outgoing circuits, some marked essential. One note card first on why one earth gives an alarm, not a trip. Jobs: a lamp goes dim, which line is it; sectionalise the board, keeping essential services on; a second earth on another line, and why that one is dangerous.
builds_on: AC circuits lesson 10 (three phases, star and delta)
Design and verification lesson 6 (shock protection and automatic disconnection on shore, for contrast)

title: A watch's defects
oneLine: When several defects come in on one watch, the dangerous one is made safe first, each is found on its own bench with the method from lessons 1 to 3, and the watch ends with a short, clear brief to the next one.
skill: Take three reports across the first three benches, solo, in an order you choose and can defend; find and prove each; leave anything not finished safe and reported; brief the next watch in four plain lines that Claude marks.
specRefs: No syllabus yet: Dan's leading rate and Level 3 marine engineering syllabi to be mapped when he shares them (brief section 9)
materialRefs: nvq-fault-finding p.1 (risk assessment; agreeing who is affected and what can stay energised)
nvq-fault-finding p.1-2 (fault codes C1 to Fi as one model of ranking danger; questions to ask)
nvq-fault-finding p.6 (leaving safe; telling the person in charge in writing)
to research: a public source on handing over unfinished work and defects between shifts or watches, without claiming Royal Navy practice
picture: No new drawing: the three benches from lessons 1 to 3 side by side, each with a fresh report from the bench's fault list. He picks the order, works each solo, and writes a four-line brief for the next watch.
